metadata.file_name: 143. Bezek Güre et al. (2023). Reviewing the Factors Affecting PISA Reading Skills by Using Random Forest and MARS Methods.pdf
metadata.title: Reviewing the Factors Affecting PISA Reading Skills by Using Random Forest and MARS Methods
metadata.venue: IJCER (International Journal of Contemporary Educational Research)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 Turkey microdata for 15-year-old students and constructs an analytic sample of 5713 students after excluding cases with missing demographic characteristics and applying additional missing-data rules at the scale level (deletion for predictors with >5% missing; regression-based handling for predictors with <5% missing). The dependent variable is derived from PISA reading plausible values (PV1READ–PV10READ) averaged to a single student-level score, then thresholded into a two-category outcome (successful vs unsuccessful). The manuscript does not report the use of PISA sampling weights or replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and it instead describes preprocessing in SPSS and model training in SPM; therefore, weighting is not documented and should be treated as potentially unweighted. Because Random Forest and MARS are applied in a standard ML workflow without explicit complex-survey correction, results may be sensitive to the omission of survey design adjustments.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 Turkey student data. A random selection of 6890 students from 186 schools (12 NUTS Level 1 regions) was drawn for the Turkey dataset; students with missing data from demographic characteristics were excluded prior to analysis. For predictors, the authors applied a missing-data procedure by scale: regression-based handling for variables with <5% missing and deletion for variables with >5% missing. The final analytic sample comprised 5713 students (2838 male, 2875 female) who took the PISA 2018 reading assessment.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (Turkey, student-level; PV1READ–PV10READ averaged; thresholded to 2 categories)
main_findings.performance_metrics: MARS vs Random Forest (classification): Correct classification rate 72.59% vs 70.28%; Sensitivity 70.51% vs 64.02%; F1 73.30% vs 69.69%; AUC 79.80% vs 78.29%; Specificity 74.96% vs 77.44%; Precision 76.32% vs 76.46%.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading data for Turkey, the study leveraged number of books at home, perception of difficulty, motivation for reading skills, father educational level, and reading pleasure to predict students’ reading skills category (successful vs unsuccessful), finding that the MARS model outperformed Random Forest on correct classification, sensitivity, F1, and AUC. This indicates that nonlinear, interaction-sensitive models may better capture how home resources and reading-related attitudes jointly relate to reading proficiency, suggesting that policy and school interventions should prioritize book access and reading motivation/difficulty supports rather than relying on linear-only assumptions, while noting that the outcome was derived from averaged PVs and the paper does not document survey-weight use.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 Turkey reading performance by predicting a binary reading skills outcome (successful vs unsuccessful) derived from averaged PV1READ–PV10READ and competence thresholds. Using 5713 students, the authors compare two supervised learners—Random Forest and MARS—trained in SPM, with predictors drawn from student background, home resources, and reading-related attitudes/experiences. Across classification metrics, MARS achieved higher correct classification (72.59% vs 70.28%), sensitivity (70.51% vs 64.02%), F1 (73.30% vs 69.69%), and AUC (79.80% vs 78.29%), while Random Forest showed higher specificity (77.44% vs 74.96%) and similar precision (76.46% vs 76.32%). The most important predictor in both models is number of books at home, followed by perception of difficulty and reading motivation/pleasure and parental education. Limitations include the use of a thresholded PV-derived DV, unclear handling of PISA complex survey weights, and the absence of explicit cross-validation/nested validation reporting in the provided text.
